A Discovery id and an option id open the proposed decision for that option.
A Discovery id without an option id lists the options with numbers. Each line shows the option id and its title. A stated number selects that option.

An invocation with neither id lists the accepted Discoveries whose Discovery ID is absent from every ADR catalog row. Each line shows the Discovery ID and its title. The list is numbered. A stated number selects that Discovery. A removed ADR row keeps that Discovery off the list.
The proposed decision is accepted before the ADR is written.
One Discovery produces at most one ADR.
The selected option is the option the person named or numbered.
The comparison and matches are copied from the Discovery.
Recommendation Override is written only when the selection differs from the recommendation.
Context states the problem and the forces. The record states what the decision covers, what it leaves open, and when to revisit it, or `None`.
Alternatives Considered includes the selected option as `Selected`, and each alternative has a definition, one outcome, and a reason.

The handoff does not repeat the selected option or the matches. The handoff contains no implementation entry. Reference Architecture is `None` when no architecture is reused, and the RA id when one is.
Relationship lines use `advances`, `bound by`, and `satisfies`, or `None`.
Status is `superseded` in the record and catalog exactly when `superseded_by` names an ADR, and the record file remains.
Authorization proceeds to Reference Architecture and does not authorize implementation.
Each id is `ADR` plus eight hex digits derived from the title.
A taken id names the conflicting titles, says a title change is appropriate, and shows a new title. The write waits until the person accepts that title.
That message does not mention identifiers, hex, sampling, or the catalog.
A failed write leaves existing ADR bytes unchanged.
The same exact option title uses the existing implementation and does not ask replace or beside. A different option title that matches one architecture asks that question once, inside the proposal.

Replacing a decision sets it to `superseded`, keeps its file, and removes it from the architecture's current decisions. Running beside adds this decision and leaves the earlier one. The architecture record and the architecture catalog show the same current decisions.
The closing message suggests exactly one next step: create the reference architecture, create the reference implementation, or the name of the implementation that already exists.
A span names every architecture in the set and does not ask which architecture to use. Leaving out architectures narrows the set. One remaining architecture asks replace or beside.
Accepting a span writes one ADR whose Architecture ID lists every RA id in the set, adds it beside each current decision, supersedes nothing, and creates no architecture.

A span close names each architecture that is not yet implemented and offers codify for one uncovered implementation at a time. A covered implementation is not offered. Opening a recorded span goes to that close and writes nothing.
The skill does not change the Discovery.

A handoff from `highway-onboarding` writes an accepted ADR without a question and returns its id. A taken id adds the provider name to the title without asking. The same title reuses the existing record.
An onboarding ADR uses `request: onboarding`, `discovery: highway`, and Discovery ID `highway`, which may appear on more than one catalog row.
An onboarding ADR uses the shared ADR sections. Discovery-only values are `None`, alternatives are headed by name, and the record contains no option id.
An onboarding handoff does not ask whether a decision replaces or runs beside another, and changes no architecture.
A missing or unknown Discovery stops the skill and writes nothing.
An option that is not in the Discovery returns to `choose-option` and writes nothing.
A second ADR for the same Discovery stops the write and shows the existing decision.
A malformed present Discovery stops the skill and writes nothing.
A failed write leaves existing ADR and catalog bytes unchanged.

Assessment opens on **What would you like to review?** with observed gaps first and ready artifacts second. Nothing is written before a choice.
Observed gaps go to the list of findings, which is unchanged.
Ready records come from the catalogs, are grouped as requests, discoveries, decisions, architectures, and implementations, and are never written as findings.
Categories are numbered and records are lettered. Each category shows at most 5 records, labeled by title and the stage it is ready for. A category with nothing ready is omitted.
The ready view asks which record to advance and always ends with the return line. Returning shows the menu again.
Advancing a record continues in the skill for its next stage. This skill does not create that record.
The default domain is `portfolio`.
Catalogs are read before source records.
Findings about providers, reuse, coverage, and dependencies use `implementations/capabilities.md` and its Parent chain.
The opening heading "Let's see what your repository may be telling us." is shown once, before the first list.

The list opens with **Based on what Highway knows, these may be worth visiting:** and shows at most 5 numbered findings, each with a title based on its Finding text, its summary, and its **Solution Complexity:**. The title is not written to the findings file.
Open findings from earlier runs come before new findings in the list.
A new finding is written with Status `Open` before it is shown.
The list asks **Would you like to explore any of these findings in more detail?** and says the person can dismiss any of them. It offers additional findings only when more remain.
Dismissing from the list sets each named finding to Status `Dismissed` and shows the list again without them.

A finding chosen by number or summary opens with **Based on what Highway knows, this may be something worth visiting:**, then the observation, then several possible solutions, an overall complexity, and a dollar cost range when one is available.
The finding asks **Would you like to explore a solution now?** and says the person can dismiss it or go back to the list of findings.
Going back, save for later, and discard each return to the list. A saved or discarded finding leaves the list.
A question about that finding is answered, then the same finding is shown again.
Save for later updates the written row to Status `Accepted`.
Discard updates the written row to Status `Dismissed`.

Explore a solution now updates the written row to Status `Accepted`, tells the person the finding is becoming a request, says they can run `highway-assessment` later, and then continues as `highway-request` at `start`. Possible solutions, complexity, and cost are not seeded.
The id is `F` plus eight hex digits derived from the observation.
The same observation reuses that id. A collision with a different observation waits for a wording change.
The findings file has no fingerprint column.
A stale revision writes nothing.
The skill creates no owner artifact.
This skill does not write a request record.
An unreadable findings file stops the skill and writes nothing.
A failed write leaves the findings file unchanged and does not show the finding.
A stale revision writes nothing.
An unsupported category or status writes nothing.
Missing evidence stays unknown and does not become a finding.

`highway-codify-config` shows the three-option menu. A platform name skips the menu and the platform list, and opens that platform's add or update or the onboard question.
`Classify` tests `edit`, `decline`, `question`, `select`, `unknown`, then `accept`, and the first match wins.
Each yes or no question answers a `question` and asks again, asks again after `unknown`, and names where `decline` goes.
A return step named by `highway-onboarding` or `highway-implementation` is held for the visit. Declining the menu goes to that step. With none held, declining the menu stops.
Picking an option and every edit begin with one consequence sentence.
Platforms and coding standards views show each catalog with list fields as ordered lists, and ask what to add, correct, or remove.
Every proposal shows its fields as bold labels, list fields as ordered lists, then Conflicts, and ends with **What would you add or correct?** and the cancel line.
A platform is added only from an accepted implementation. Any other name offers onboarding, which ends by pointing back here.
Accepting a platform writes only its row. Accepting a standard writes its file, then its row. Removing a standard keeps its file.

A standard proposal shows its File and Folder Structure as relative paths. Accepting one with no path, a path beginning with `/` or `code/`, or a required test path outside the structure writes nothing and says what is needed.
No coding standard is seeded. The first accepted standard adds its row to the seeded catalog.
Conflicts quote both entries and name both records. With none, the person is asked what inconsistencies they noticed.
A resolution lists each record in bold with lettered changes, writes only those changes, and returns to the reassessed list.
A cancel writes nothing and returns to the menu.
`current` is read before an add or update, and a removal does not run it.

On an add, `entry level` proposes one to four classes of automation for each of When to use and When not to use, from what `current` describes, and no task. `use entries` writes each as one condition or one outcome in five words or fewer, and keeps saved entries on an update. Each proposal entry has a blank line, then **Why it matters:** stating its consequence, and the saved catalog does not keep that line.
An add or update proposal with no edit yet, for a platform or a standard, shows the starting-point line after the consequence sentence. An edited proposal and a remove do not.
A standard add or update follows `standard rules`, then `use entries`. A remove runs neither.

`current` groups the automation capabilities the platform documentation describes by meaning. Each group the implementation does not already mean appears once under New Realized Capabilities, with the product and the handoff in the evidence. After the write, configuration follows `highway-implementation` to record them, with the return step `platform written`.

Each coding rule is one must, one condition, and one outcome in eight words or fewer. The model suggests at most fifteen, and one keeps encoded or encrypted credentials outside the files. A provided rule that does not conform is rewritten, and the opening consequence sentence names the rewrite. Each rule shows **Why it matters:** on the proposal only.
A standard write with no conflicts states one consequence sentence and returns to the menu.
A missing template stops the change, names the template path, and writes nothing.
A failed write leaves the existing file unchanged and keeps the proposal open.
A failed standard file write writes no catalog row.
A standard with no structure path, a path that is not relative, or a required test path outside the structure writes nothing and keeps the proposal open.
A name that is not an accepted implementation is not added and offers onboarding.

An exact title selects that accepted implementation, and the title is what the person sees.
A supplied id selects the matching accepted implementation, and the title is shown afterward.
A list shows a title and the implementation summary. It does not use an id as the label.
One to five accepted implementations are listed when the person names nothing. More than five lists none until the person gives a title or a description, then at most five.
No accepted implementation writes nothing.

With no named action, the suggestion list appears once before any proposal. It opens with the one Technology Choice, or the implementation title, and says automating these tasks may be worth visiting.

Each suggestion title is an action that starts with a verb, and its one summary sentence expands on it. The list holds at most five items, uses no id as a label, and ends with the invitation to describe another idea.
With no instance running, `Establish [implementation title]` comes first. Every other suggestion comes from one realized capability, in Realized Capabilities order.

A suggestion already in a product that lists this implementation is left out before the list keeps five: by a recorded feature with the same words, ignoring case, or by a feature sentence or product Summary with that meaning. No product folder is opened. Removed rows and integration rows leave nothing out.

The proposal shows **Proposed project:** as `New <folder>` or `Existing <folder>`, then **Rationale:**. Its first sentence is plain language. A standard or integration is cited only when it replaced the decision.

The person's project edit is written. The folder stays unique, including removed rows, the `CDY` id is in `.highway/metadata.md`, the feature is under `.highway/features/`, and paths are relative to the folder.

Each accepted action is the next numbered feature directory in its product, numbered from the last row of the Features table in `.highway/metadata.md`. No features folder is listed. Earlier directories stay.
Each accepted feature adds one Features row with its number, folder, title, and Summary. A row is never removed.
Features keeps an entry only when that feature starts the product, adds an implementation, records an integration, changes the summary, or is open.
Accepting a proposal that includes an integration writes one row to `code/integrations.md`, and a pair already accepted writes none.
A named action skips the suggestion list and opens the proposal for that action.

Before any proposal, coding standards are checked first and vendor documentation second. Corrections and inconclusive results are named before the proposal and are not saved. The checks keep the selected action.
A standard that cannot be met for the selected action shows no proposal and returns to suggestions.
The proposal shows Title, Summary, Description, Acceptance criteria, Diagram, and Tasks, in that order. It shows no components, current state, separate action, day, or means.

The diagram is one logical flow, top to bottom, from the Provider. Each arrow leaves the Provider, is one task's action, starts with a verb, and points to that task's target, in task order. No arrow leaves a target.

Every task names the same Provider, the platform executing the automation. The implementation being automated is a target. A Shopify proposal can use Cursor when Cursor is included, even though the Shopify records do not name it.

A named platform with no catalog row stays the Provider and the proposal says `highway-codify-config` can add it. With no row and no named platform, the proposal says a platform is needed and accept stays on `revise`.

After a selection, a record whose Deployed by or Managed by is `Needed`, empty, or has no row, or whose Language is `Needed`, empty, or has no row, emits the missing critical detail line and "Let's set those details now for [Product Title].", then follows `highway-implementation` with the return step `record check`. It asks no question and holds no platform for one run.
A return with the record still incomplete stops and writes nothing.

An implementation whose Language names a coding standard is a code project. Until an Establish feature is recorded, `Establish [implementation title]` is the only suggestion, even when an instance is running. Later suggestions come from Realized Capabilities, Realized Interfaces, covered Coverage rows, then NFR Realization, at most five.

A code project's Establish proposes the project structure, the build file, the entry point, the configuration, and a health check, plus pipeline tasks when Deployed by is a pipeline. A code task shows Language in place of Provider. The Executor is Deployed by.
A code project's product is titled from the implementation, lists only that implementation, and its close says the code was not run.

Each task shows Standards as an ordered list, or `No coding standard applies.` A standard whose When not to use matches is dropped. A standard comes before the standards it inherits from, and each inherited standard appears once.
A Standards edit re-emits the proposal with one consequence sentence. A title not in the catalog is left out and points to `highway-codify-config`.
`align` corrects the method, library, module, or pattern against every standard on the task's list and keeps the Provider.
An invocation of the word `configure` points to `highway-codify-config` and writes nothing.

`highway-codify catalog` lists at most five accepted automations, newest first, with each implementation title and progress, says how many more exist, and writes nothing. A selection shows the files path and the README path.
A new row in `code/code.md` is appended as the last row.
The README is headed `## Setup Instructions`, then `## User Guide`.
A finished run closes with the completion message, both paths, and the sentence that the automation was not run. A stopped run names the stopped task and does not say the codify stage is complete.
Each task is one action against one target and shows Scope, Provider, Method, Standards, Files, and Assumptions.

Files lists relative paths placed from the File and Folder Structure of the task's standards. A listed standard with no structure is named before the proposal with a pointer to `highway-codify-config`. A Files edit changes only this automation. An unfilled placeholder keeps the proposal open.
A second action waits for another run. Declining writes nothing. Accepting is the only confirmation.

Acceptance writes `codify.md`, the product's `metadata.md` with the new Features row, the catalog row, and any new integrations row together, then `plan.md`. It writes no task list, no file the task list names, and no README.
The proposal heading is `Here is a proposed starting point for your codify feature:`. `Highway will use this specification to build out the solution.` follows `If this is accurate, just say so.`
The menu offers Review the plan and Continue to code the solution. A feature with a plan and no task list resumes at the menu.

Reviewing the plan reads every section, then asks **What would you add, correct, or remove?** and "If this is accurate, just say so." before the menu returns. Accepting emits the menu, and a change regenerates the plan and runs `check`. Continuing to code asks no review question.
Continuing emits the building sentence once, then writes the task list ordered by story, each heading with its independent test.
The task list follows `codify-tasks.md`. A story's test line comes first only when its first standard says `Tests: required`.

Coding starts with no question after the task list is written. Every standard a task names, and each existing file it names, is read before its files are written, and no other automation file is read, the earlier one winning a disagreement, and each task is marked `[X]` before the next begins.
A task that cannot be finished stops the run with that task and every later task open. The next run starts at the first open task, redoes no finished task, and runs no check.
Codify creates, edits, and removes no coding standard and no row of the coding standards catalog.
Acceptance and coding run the automation zero times and leave the implementation, architecture, decision, request, and finding unchanged.

A Reference Architecture id for an accepted architecture opens the proposed realization.

An invocation without an id lists every accepted architecture. Each line shows the Architecture ID, its title, and how many current implementations it has. The list is numbered. A stated number selects that architecture. A removed implementation row does not count as current.

Declining a proposal writes nothing, and existing implementations stay as they were.
An architecture that is not accepted writes nothing.

The proposed realization is accepted before the record is written.

Coverage rows are the architecture's stated responsibilities. Conformance is `compatible` when every row is covered or not applicable, and that record has no gap section and no conflict section. An uncovered responsibility is `incomplete` and states the gap.

`implementations/capabilities.md` is written in the same step, with ID, Parent, Title, and Realized By.
Each capability title follows the capability title rule. A title that joins two things becomes two capabilities without a question, and the consequence sentence names the compounding effect.

The record contains no plans, tasks, source code, or infrastructure definitions.

The implementation title is the decision's product or named mechanism, without "Adopt". The proposal shows it before acceptance. It gains "for" and the purpose only when that title belongs to an implementation of a different architecture.
The catalog index columns are Implementation ID, Architecture ID, Implementation Title, Implementation Path, and Status.
A taken id names the conflicting titles, says a title change is appropriate, and shows a new title. The write waits until the person accepts that title.

An accepted implementation that can start automation, such as an agent that starts the work, gets one row in `library/coding-standards/codify-platforms.md` with blank When to use and When not to use. The person is told it is included and asked whether to configure how highway-codify uses it. A yes emits "Let's configure how highway-codify uses [Platform]." and follows `highway-codify-config` for that platform with the return step `close`. A no goes to `close`. Under `onboarding`, the step returns to highway-onboarding after the write, without the included line or the question.
